Although learning-based approaches have proven effective in enhancing medical images, existing methods often fail to generalize well across diverse artifacts and produce outputs unsuitable for precise tumor assessment. Furthermore, existing studies lack human expert validation of their enhancements, particularly regarding the ability of these enhancements to accurately delineate tumors amidst varying artifact severities and types. Furthermore, studies by experts confirm the utility of the generated high-frequency component images for the accurate identification of esophageal tumors.

This research examines whether web crawlers—the algorithms that index and retrieve online content—also contribute to the viral nature of misinformation. An analysis of nearly 13 million crawled pages containing fake news shows that crawlers are responsible for spreading approximately one-third of these stories to points beyond their initial domains. The findings reveal that while these machines aim for neutral indexing, the inherent structure of the online ecosystem drives the over-sampling of sensationalist material. Furthermore, because crawlers operate continuously, they ensure that even time-sensitive false claims remain available indefinitely. This automatic mechanism offers a plausible explanation for why misinformation, even from transient events, persists across the internet without ongoing human effort.

We present a specific class of 3-knots involving a single crossing where the 3-knot behaves like a closed string wrapped around a torus, termed T-3-knots. We demonstrate that any T-3-knot is characterized by a unique canonical form, established through a one-to-one correspondence between these knots and positive integers via an explicitly defined algorithm. Our results indicate that functional genes rapidly emerge and are selected for in nature upon the initial appearance of a protein T-3-knot. This study provides original insights into protein knot development life cycles and the broader field of molecular evolution theory.

Likelihood Estimation (MLE) pre-training is a popular strategy to boost resource efficiency, the associated benefits often remain sub-optimal. This paper investigates such limitations within the specific context of Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging. Our findings reveal that the primary limitation stems not from the RL method itself, but rather from the training data used for RL, which remains flawed due to inaccuracies from the initial MLE model. These RL datasets contain a high volume of false corrections arising from RL policies that overly smooth coarse-grained predictions, thereby solidifying significant errors. We demonstrate the efficacy of addressing this by introducing "Guarded Policy," an approach designed specifically to curtail false improvements. When applied to the Character-level LSTM POS tagger, Guarded Policy achieves a 21.33% drop in mean errors per sentence on the RL training corpus, an enhancement that translates to a 3.33% test set accuracy gain (measured as a reduction in errors) for the CNN/Coling-shaped linguistic challenge.

Large Hadron Collider (LHC) initiated its upgrade, now known as the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC), designed to boost beam luminosity by a factor of ten relative to current levels. This initiative prompted European nuclear physicists to develop projects for new detectors capable of operating under high-luminosity conditions to study mesons and baryons. One such venture is the Nucleon Photon Interactions and Structure with High-Luminosity (NPS-HL) detector, which focuses on exploring the non-perturbative regime of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). NPS-HM aims to investigate in-medium modifications of hadron properties within nuclear matter, as well as intrinsic and orbital quark and gluon contributions to the nucleon structure through deep inelastic scattering (DIS) processes. Complementarily, this document outlines the Monte Carlo simulation framework employed in the NPS-HM project to model detector performance and precision within DIS and single pion production channels within the specified HL goals.

the joint evolution of a host population and its pathogen. The host evolves to maximize the rate of transmission avoidance, while the pathogen counter-adapts to maximize its spread within the host. Initially, both groups possess a simple, homogeneous trait structure; however, as selection pressures intensify, these populations differentiate into distinct subgroups based on host immunity and infectiousness, respectively. This dynamic frequently yields complex, spatially varying patterns of host and pathogen stratification that mirror real-world epidemics driven by evolving microbial strains. Although such outcomes are plausible, they are by no means guaranteed; both host and pathogen may instead collapse, allowing the infectious agent to reach epidemic levels of virulence that kill the host population entirely. Ultimately, the system's trajectory hinges critically on specific parameters, particularly the intensity of host-to-pathogen killing, which can tip the balance toward mutual coexistence or total mutual destruction.

patient health improvements calls for a fundamental rethinking of how medical knowledge is generated, shared, and applied. The model achieves optimal internal consistency when the Higgs boson exhibits full Standard Model interactions at $2\sigma$ precision levels. For the specific case where the ratio of Standard Electromagnetic to Standard Weak interaction reaches the range of 80–100%, the parameter space demonstrates heightened internal coherence. If future measurements confirm this ratio of $\lambda$ falls precisely at 2$\sigma$ precision levels, the SM framework would demonstrate significant internal consistency without requiring extensions.

Designed to handle large-scale applications, it integrates a diverse array of geometric representations alongside advanced statistical techniques, machine learning algorithms, and user-defined analytical modules. Furthermore, the system supports interactive 3D and 2D desktop environments featuring hexagonal, radial, and tree-like hexagonal layouts. A standout capability is its "Splitter" technology, which dynamically partitions the 3D workspace into hexagonal prisms to effectively display extensive datasets while enabling users to inspect individual attributes of data points directly within 3D subviews. viDaExpert operates as a versatile desktop environment, offering features like a dynamic interface with draggable windows, an extensible plugin architecture, and a robust API for developing new visualization formats and utilities. Initial deployments of this system include use cases in genomics and energy flow analysis.
